Let <MATH_0001> be a topological space.
Let <MATH_0002> be an abelian presheaf on <MATH_0003>.
Then there exists a unique structure of
abelian sheaf on <MATH_0004> such that
<MATH_0005> is a morphism
of abelian presheaves. Moreover, the following adjointness
property holds
<MATH_0006>

Recall the sheaf of sets <MATH_0001> defined in
Section <REF_0001>. All the stalks
<MATH_0002> are abelian groups, see
Lemma <REF_0002>.
Hence <MATH_0003> is a sheaf of abelian groups by
Example <REF_0003>.
Also, it is clear that the map <MATH_0004>
is a morphism of abelian presheaves. If we show that
condition <MATH_0005> of Section <REF_0004> defines a subgroup
of <MATH_0006> for all open subsets <MATH_0007>,
then <MATH_0008> canonically inherits the structure of abelian sheaf.
This is quite easy to do by hand, and we leave it to the
reader to find a good simple argument. The argument we use here,
which generalizes to presheaves of algebraic structures is the following:
Lemma <REF_0005> show that
<MATH_0009> is the fibre product of a diagram
of abelian groups. Thus <MATH_0010> is an abelian
subgroup as desired.

<STRUCT_0001><STRUCT_0002>
Note that at this point <MATH_0011> is an abelian
group by Lemma <REF_0006>
and that <MATH_0012> is a
bijection (Lemma <REF_0007>)
and a homomorphism of abelian groups. Hence
<MATH_0013> is an isomorphism
of abelian groups. This will be used below without further mention.

<STRUCT_0003><STRUCT_0004>
To prove the adjointness property we use the adjointness
property of sheafification of presheaves of sets. For example
if <MATH_0014> is morphism of presheaves
then we obtain a morphism of sheaves
<MATH_0015>. What we have to do is to check
that this is a morphism of abelian sheaves. We may do this
for example by noting that it is true on stalks,
by Lemma <REF_0008>, and then using
Lemma <REF_0009> above.
